author: EDRi
title: EDRi-gram, 19 November 2026
content:
What has the EDRi network been up to over the past few weeks? Find out the latest digital rights news in our regular newsletter. In this edition: Making sense of the Digital Fairness Act, a very unmerry birthday to the Digital Omnibus, and more!

Last week, the European Commission put digital fairness on the menu with a proposal for its long-awaited Digital Fairness Act (DFA) – and we have some food for thought.

This law will strengthen consumer protection against manipulative and exploitative commercial practices, such as fake notifications designed to keep bringing us back to an app, endless scrolling that keeps us online way longer than you intended, and other personalised techniques used by online services that exploit our vulnerabilities. First things first, proposal actually takes some important steps forward by introducing new prohibitions on deceptive design, extending specific protections beyond the biggest online platforms, and recognising the harms associated with addictive digital features. However, we were left wondering – why promise digital fairness yet leave the users to do all the work instead of holding manipulative online services responsible? Read our analysis on Tech Policy Press.

author: EDRi
title: New report documents authoritarian use of technology across the globe
content:
Privacy International's latest report documents how states are deploying authoritarian technology to stifle dissent, assert control and diminish human rights. The report conveys how surveillance technologies are being expanded and entrenched with the purpose of exerting control over entire populations and/or specific groups of people such as journalists and human rights defenders.

By Privacy International (guest author) · November 19, 2026

EDRi-member Privacy International (PI) have been observing and monitoring an increase in states’ adoption of authoritarian practices and policies. These practices are facilitated by new and emerging technologies or embodied in their very deployment to stifle dissent, assert control and diminish human rights. These digital technologies, such as facial recognition, social media monitoring, spyware, and more, are being deployed — both online and offline — by authoritarian and democratic regimes alike. PI have coined the term ‘authoritarian use of technology’ to describe this global phenomenon.

PI believes that the authoritarian use of technology goes beyond the unlawful use or abuse of technologies by states that the organisation has been monitoring and exposing for years. Authoritarian use of tech results in a systematic undermining of democratic principles, erosion of the rule of law, exertion of significant social and political control, or normalisation of the surveillance of individuals and their communities – particularly those already at risk.

These technologies are being expanded and entrenched with the purpose of exerting control over entire populations and groups of people at risk, such as human rights defenders (HRDs), journalists, lawyers, activists, dissidents and those from minority ethnic, national and religious backgrounds. This is being done to target, persecute or ostracise them. This ultimately creates a ‘chilling effect’, spreading a fear of reprisal, which serves not only to infringe upon the rights of certain individuals, but of whole communities and populations. In turn, this has a corrosive effect on democratic institutions, mechanisms of accountability, oversight and redress, and the fabric of open societies.

In their new report, PI examine the use of five technologies: facial recognition technology, mobile phone extraction, spyware, social media and intelligence monitoring, and mass communications surveillance. The report also provides several cross-cutting themes emerging from the authoritarian use of these technologies on human rights. These include: a systemic interference with the right to privacy, the erosion of and chilling effect on enjoyment of broader fundamental rights and freedoms, the disproportionate or discriminatory targeting of certain groups in society, the absence of clear legal basis, effective safeguards, and independent oversight, and lastly, the lack of accountability of private sector actors.

Facial recognition technology (FRT) is a technology that uses a camera to capture images of people’s faces and then extracts and processes their biometric data to verify an individual or identify a match against an existing image. The report collates examples of how governments and law enforcement are deploying FRT at protests to identify, monitor and track protesters either openly or surreptitiously, and even banning wearing face coverings at protests to facilitate it. The report also features case studies of FRT projects in the UK, Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territories, and Brazil.

PI’s report includes a chapter on mobile phone extraction, which documents the technology being deployed to gather information and intelligence about activists, journalists, political dissidents, and migrants, which they believe to constitute an authoritarian use of the technology. Our electronic devices, such as our mobile phones and tablets, contain huge amounts of information and sensitive data about our lives. Mobile phone extraction involves extracting data from an individual’s device, or from the cloud services they use, including device information, photos, videos, audio recordings, notes, documents and apps used, as well as the messages, call logs and emails they draft, send and receive.

The report also gathers examples of spyware repeatedly being deployed by both authoritarian and democratic governments to conduct secret, intrusive surveillance of journalists, human rights defenders, opposition politicians, their family members and other individuals already at risk of state repression. Spyware is a huge intrusive surveillance technology that can secretly get everything from a person’s phone: messages, photos, contacts, location, microphone, camera, and browsing history, without them ever knowing. The report refers to the NSO Group and The Pegasus Scandal, and examples from across the Gulf countries of Bahrain, United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.

The report also includes social media intelligence monitoring as a tool increasingly being used by governments and non-state actors for exercising authoritarian control. It draws on the US Department of State’s screening and vetting process of student visa applicants to include applicants’ social media, as well as its use to monitor and track government dissent and protestors in Colombia, the UK and Mexico.

Lastly, PI’s report covers the use of mass communications interception as posing one of the most significant intrusions for privacy, as it can be directed not just at specific individuals but at entire populations. Communications interception is the monitoring, interception, collection, preservation and retention of information that has been communicated, relayed or generated over communications networks by a third party such as law enforcement agency, intelligence agency, a private company, or a malicious actor. The report explains how International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) catchers, which function by mimicking nearby mobile cell towers and intercept communications and location data transmitted by personal communication devices, are being used to intercept protester’s communications and devices in the USA and allegedly the UK. The use of Bulk Communications Interception in Libya provides another example of what may be referred to as an authoritarian use of tech.

Across their analysis of states’ deployment of such technologies, PI found that legislative, technical and regulatory safeguards to oversee the deployment of such technologies were weak, incomplete, unenforced, lacking entirely, or even explicitly serving to bolster and uphold their weaponisation as tools of oppression. Therefore, they conclude each chapter with a specific set of safeguards and restrictions pertaining to each technology that are required to restrict their use to ways that comply with human rights law. However, PI also concludes that certain technologies are so inherently intrusive by design that they are incapable of being reconciled with human rights standards. In particular, they believe that live FRT and mass communications interception exemplify this category of disproportionately intrusive technologies.

The collated case studies and examples of how these technologies are being used illustrates that these are not isolated incidents but part of a wider emerging global trend – the rise of the authoritarian use of technology as a phenomenon that is cutting across borders, cultures and jurisdictions.

PI will continue to monitor developments and raise awareness about the intrusive and devastating impact that the authoritarian use of technology can have on the enjoyment of human rights. They will continue to advocate for the necessary safeguards and restrictions that should be implemented to ensure states do not misuse and abuse these technologies.

Contribution by: Sarah Simms, Senior Policy Officer, Privacy International

Privacy International, Global Report on the Authoritarian use of Technology, October 2026

author: EDRi
title: EU transforms Frontex into a high-tech deportation command centre
content:
On 27 October 2026, the European Commission tabled a new Regulation for Frontex, the EU's border agency, expanding its powers and refocusing its mandate on deportations, preventing arrivals, and surveillance beyond EU territories and into social media. This would effectively turn Frontex into the EU's deportation agency, equivalent of ICE in the United States.

By Protect Not Surveil Coalition (guest author) · November 19, 2026

At the centre of this reform is a budget that would almost double to nearly €12 billion for 2028–2034, leading to a massive expansion of the EU security and surveillance industrial complex. Frontex will test and deploy new technology to repress migrants, funnelling billions of taxpayer money to surveillance, security and defence contractors. EU’s hostile border security regime has for years produced systemic and massive human rights violations of migrants, refugees and racialised people, and those who stand in solidarity with them. This proposal will accelerate that.

The proposal operationalises the recently adopted Deportations Regulation and deepens Frontex’s position as the central actor of a Europe-wide deportation machine. This will make the agency responsible for collecting and analysing data from Member States in order to “predict” deportation needs, and allocating resources to them. Frontex will now have a “Deportation Coordination Centre” that is expected to act at all stages of the deportation procedure, from detecting and identifying people that may be expulsed, booking or arranging flights and escorts, to monitoring their “reintegration” in the destination country.

Alarmingly, it expands Frontex’s powers to deport outside of the EU’s borders. Based on a simple status agreement, Frontex will be able to deport people from one third country to another, with the aim of preventing people from even reaching the EU. This will likely mean sharing sensitive data with third countries and countries of origin, where individuals may be at risk of persecution or harm.

The Frontex mandate reform comes in a package with a proposal to digitalise the management of deportation cases. The border control agency is given a key role in the harmonised technical design of EU and national digital systems, to exchange data on deportations, including sensitive data transfers to third countries (biometric data, travel documents and history, grounds for deportation, health data, etc.), and automate certain steps of the procedure, such as adding deportation orders in the Schengen Information System (SIS) to detect people.

With this reform, Frontex’s practice of “debriefing interviews” is codified, particularly during the screening procedure introduced by the Migration Pact. The agency conducts these covert “voluntary” interrogations of people immediately after they disembark or cross the border. During these interviews, the agency extracts data from migrants deemed to be “suspects” of “cross-border crime”, without the possibility for migrants to seek legal counsel. Debriefing interviews have been rightfully criticised for their absence of fundamental rights monitoring and their unfairness as they take place when a person is detained and lacks privacy.

A new “Online Monitoring and Response Centre” will also surveil social media platforms to identify “suspicious behaviours or trends” in people’s movements at the EU borders, and before that, in the countries of origin and transit. Aggregated data collected online will be fed into Frontex’s “risk analysis” to guide border forces’ deployment and reaction. Social media monitoring was already declared as carrying high-risk for violating the fundamental rights of people affected, and was banned by the European Data Protection Supervisor in 2019 when first implemented by the EU Agency for Asylum.

Frontex will also seek designation as a trusted flagger under the Digital Services Act (DSA), allowing the agency to report pieces of online content to platforms for removal, effectively giving the agency extrajudicial powers to police the internet. It may also recommend national authorities to issue binding take-down notices. Frontex depriving people from finding legal support, sharing their stories or expressing solidarity is undoubtedly a serious infringement of freedom of expression.

All information collected during debriefings and online monitoring activities will contribute to Frontex’s border surveillance intelligence gathering called “European situational picture”. It may be combined with data from EUROSUR, Frontex’s information exchange framework with national border authorities, whose scope has been extended to include personal data in supposedly “exceptional” cases. Very sensitive data such as facial images, age, gender, physical and mental state may be processed to provide “situational awareness in situations posing imminent threat to the integrity of the external borders”. This could mean that individuals can be identified and targeted through cross-checking with OSINT data or AI-based identification tools like facial recognition.

Under the pretence of fighting the “facilitation of migration”, Europol, the EU’s policing agency, will be able to routinely consult personal data collected by Frontex. This could lead to individuals involved in border crossings, as survivors or supporters, to mistakenly fall under the investigation of Europol possibly with serious consequences, including impacts on their access to legal stay, detention, deportation or even criminal charges.

Frontex will now also be able to deploy a “Quick Reaction Force”, to react “flexibly” to “crisis and emergency situations” at EU borders. In this case, flexibility means outside of the usual controls and safeguards. Rather than coordinating humanitarian responses and triggering the solidarity mechanisms Member States agreed upon in the Migration Pact, the Reaction Force will likely aim to quickly and violently deport and force out people who are arriving to seek protection.

The reform explicitly gives Frontex powers to research, test, and procure new technologies, including AI-enabled tools, drones, sensors and digital analytics. The agency will now be able to run trials, validate products and then procure them at scale, acting in some cases as a central purchasing body for Member States to pool technical equipment, while supplying non-EU countries with more repressive tools. This will reinforce global business for digital surveillance tech and arms, making migration repression a market of its own. The use of such technologies aims to prevent people from even reaching the EU, further outsourcing EU’s responsibility for border deaths and fundamental rights violations to private security companies and non-EU governments.

The Commission frames migration as a “hybrid threat”, “instrumentalisation” and “weaponisation”, citing events such as Ceuta in 2026 to justify emergency powers and the expansion of Frontex’s surveillance capacities. This dangerous framing conflates individuals as security threats and removes their agency in their decision to move.

For decades, European governments and the EU have responded to migration not by addressing inequality, conflict, climate change, or the reasons people move, but by expanding a militarised border regime. Europe does not need a deportation agency. It does not need ICE. It needs a different approach to human movement: one that recognises movement as a human reality, protects people’s rights, and invests in safety, solidarity and community rather than deterrence and control.

The choice is between a Europe that responds to challenges through militarisation and exclusion, and one that responds through dignity, care, and shared responsibility.

"With the new Frontex reform, the EU seems committed to making its borders even more deadly than they already are for people who come seeking safety and protection. The Commission has given a massive boost to the shady surveillance practices of Frontex by doubling their budget and loosening the already-lax data protection rules. The newly introduced social media surveillance, secret interrogations at borders, AI-powered sensors collecting data in real-time will all equip Fortress Europe for illegal pushbacks, more surveillance, and more misery."

"The Frontex regulation announced yesterday shows that impunity pays. Not only is Frontex able to receive new powers and a massive funding boost to expand its border surveillance apparatus, it can do so with full immunity for human rights violations and pushbacks that have and will continue to happen under its watch. It is deeply concerning how far the Commission is prepared to go to stop people from reaching safety and building a life in Europe."

"In the most substantial reform of Frontex to date, the EU transforms the agency into the central operations room for its deportation regime, with broader surveillance powers complemented by a bigger standing army.

Doubling Frontex's budget to bolster kidnappings, prisons and ICE-like systems comes at a time when Europe's social systems are failing. The EU is cynically distracting us from the real problems – cost of living, failure of social services and the climate crisis."

"The new Frontex reform builds on years of unchecked privileged relationship between Frontex and the arms and tech companies, as in the case of Frontex Industry Days, which gave the private sector abundant face time to pitch their products and set the Agency's priorities. Frontex will enable big profits from deadly deportation regime."

"This proposal massively expands Frontex's powers to track, control and deport undocumented people, from inside the EU to third countries and between third countries, without introducing stronger human rights safeguards. All this for an agency with a track record of allegations of complicity in fundamental rights violations.

Deportation operations and immigration detention centres in the EU are already rife with abuse, and we fear that expanding Frontex's role will exacerbate these abuses within the EU and extend them beyond its borders. This proposal reflects a political obsession with deportations that ignores the realities of migration and Europe's own economies."

“At least 12 lives were lost in two shipwrecks last week and in both cases the Hellenic Coast Guards, who deploy Frontex Assets, were involved. Frontex clearly fails its human rights monitoring obligations when such incidents are so prevalent. We are deeply concerned that Frontex’s Mandate could be expanded, when what is actually needed is adequate search and rescue, accountability and safe routes.”

author: EDRi
title: One year later, a broad coalition tells EU lawmakers: do not simplify away people’s rights with the Digital Omnibus
content:
On 19 November 2025, the European Commission presented the Digital Omnibus as an exercise in simplification. One year later, 100 organisations and individuals from across civil society are warning that simplification is turning into deregulation, with consequences far beyond the usual digital-rights debate.

A new open letter calls on EU lawmakers to protect data protection, privacy and other fundamental rights, rather than weakening them in the name of empty promises of competitiveness and the AI hype.

There are plenty of things about EU digital regulation that could genuinely be simpler: people should not have to fight through endless cookie banners, regulators should cooperate better, businesses should not operate in good faith knowing other companies won’t be held accountable when disrespecting the law…

But cutting red tape and cutting rights are not the same thing. The Digital Omnibus proposed, amongst other, significant changes to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and ePrivacy framework. These affect when information about us is protected, how companies may reuse personal data for AI, safeguards around automated decision-making, access and transparency rights, and protection against unwanted access to our devices.

content:

While EDRi is still in the process of finalising its position and recommendations for this file, there are certain elements which are very clear already. We invite all readers of the EDRi-gram to submit a short opinion to the consultation, open until 3 December at midnight, covering at least the following points:

author: EDRi
title: Open Letter: EDRi warns of EU’s undemocratic attempt to introduce surveillance in satellite-based communications
content:
The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union are currently negotiating two laws to regulate communications service providers, including satellite-based ones. In both laws, the Commission has sneakily attempted to attribute itself the possibility to impose intrusive surveillance, notably data retention and interception obligations, on those satellite operators through opaque procedures. EDRi and its members warns against these unchecked powers and asks the Parliament and the Council to stand for fundamental rights and the EU’s principles for good law-making.

EDRi and members concerned about attempt to introduce unlawful data retention obligations

EDRi and its members are writing to the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union to express their serious concerns about the attempt to introduce unlawful data retention obligations through EU authorisation procedures for satellite operators under the Digital Networks Act (DNA) and Mobile Satellite Services (MSS) Regulation proposals.

In short, the Commission could impose data retention and interception obligations on satellite operators and define their modalities through a comitology procedure, which is shrouded in secrecy. author: EDRi
title: 1,840 amendments, one basic question: will the Data Omnibus simplify EU digital rules or weaken people’s rights?
content:
The European Parliament is considering 1,840 amendments to the Digital Omnibus on Data, a proposal that would change the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), ePrivacy and other parts of the EU’s data rules. We have analysed the amendments related to data protection and privacy. Our new guide shows that Parliament faces a choice between genuine simplification that makes rights easier to exercise and changes that would make more (ab)uses of personal data easier while weakening safeguards and exponentially deepening legal uncertainty.

The European Commission presented the Digital Omnibus proposal in November 2025 as a way to simplify EU digital regulation. Yet the proposal reopens fundamental questions about when the GDPR applies and what protections people receive, from the definition of personal data to artificial intelligence (AI), automated decisions, access rights and tracking technologies.

The debate has now moved to the European Parliament. Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) tabled 1,762 amendments on top of the 78 changes in the joint LIBE-ITRE draft report. Together, the 1,840 amendments show a much wider political argument about what EU data protection and privacy should become.

Our analysis identifies three broad directions: some amendments would restore or strengthen existing safeguards, others improve parts of the Commission proposal while leaving the underlying problems in place, and a third group creates new exclusions, permissions or institutional shortcuts that push the file further towards substantive deregulation.

Some of the most consequential amendments concern the definition of personal data. Proposals allowing the same information to fall inside or outside the GDPR depending on which organisation holds it could make protection depend increasingly on how companies organise data chains. This risks creating more disputes about whether the GDPR applies before people can even exercise the rights it gives them.

Another major fight concerns AI and personal data. The Commission proposes a dedicated provision recognising AI development and operation as a context for legitimate-interest processing. Article 6 of the GDPR already allows legitimate interests where the ordinary legal test is satisfied. A dedicated AI route could instead give one technology a privileged legal signal, and several amendments would expand that route further.

The Parliament seem more protective in some other areas: several amendments seek to preserve access and transparency rights, meaningful safeguards against automated decisions and a stronger role for independent data-protection authorities. These proposals are important because simplification should reduce friction without changing the substance of a right.

The clearest example is binding privacy signals: people could communicate a durable tracking choice once through browsers, operating systems or apps, instead of confronting repeated consent banners. The amendment pattern suggests that most parliamentary models retain some form of privacy signal, although MEPs disagree about its legal effect, scope and timing. This is exactly the kind of simplification worth pursuing.

There are other useful ideas too, including common tools for data protection impact assessments, clearer complaint pathways, streamlined reporting and stronger European Data Protection Board (EDPB) coordination. These approaches show that reducing unnecessary complexity does not require weaker rights. Our earlier analysis of the Commission proposal and our separate positions on GDPR safeguards and ePrivacy set out the broader concerns.

We continue to believe that the Digital Omnibus on Data should be rejected as a whole. Reopening fundamental rights legislation through a horizontal simplification exercise remains the wrong approach. The Council position agreed on 21 October 2026, mostly aligned with deregulation, makes the Parliament’s choices even more important.

If the Parliament nevertheless continues with the proposal, the test should be simple: simplify procedures and make rights easier to exercise and enforce. MEPs should reject amendments that narrow substantive protections or create new data-use privileges, and support changes that remove duplication while keeping the underlying safeguards intact.

Our new guide reads the amendment packages issue by issue, rather than treating amendment numbers in isolation. It is designed to help MEPs, civil society and everyone whose rights are affected understand what each approach would mean in practice.

author: EDRi
title: Data retention is mass surveillance of people’s phone and internet activity
content:
In 2014, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) declared mass retention of internet traffic and location data as contrary to the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Any proposal for a new EU instrument harmonising data retention must respect the boundaries of CJEU jurisprudence and uphold the rights to privacy, data protection and freedom of expression. Read more in EDRi’s new publication.

It is the legal requirement for internet service providers to retain metadata about their users beyond what is necessary for the provision of the service (e.g. billing or network optimisation and security purposes) and to keep it solely so that it can later be accessed by law enforcement bodies and intelligence services.

Metadata is data generated for the purpose of transmitting content in electronic communications services and networks. This includes mobile numbers of the sender and recipient, the time and duration of a call or an internet session, websites accessed, and the location of mobile devices. On a technical level, metadata is no longer needed once the transmission ends.

Metadata is very revealing about people’s private lives.

author: EDRi
title: EU governments call it ‘simplification,’ but their Data Omnibus deal considerably weakens our rights
content:
EU governments have agreed on their position on the Digital Omnibus, retaining changes that threaten fundamental rights to privacy and data protection. With negotiations moving to the European Parliament, MEPs must reject the proposed weakening of GDPR safeguards for AI and pseudonymised data, protect individual rights, and defend ePrivacy against new tracking exemptions. Genuine simplification should make our rights easier to exercise and enforce, not give companies more freedom to exploit our data.

When the European Commission presented its Digital Omnibus in November 2025, it promised to simplify Europe’s digital rules without weakening fundamental rights. Yet, as EDRi and others warned at the time, a majority of its proposals, particularly those regarding General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and ePrivacy, went far beyond reducing administrative burdens. They are part and parcel of a broad deregulatory wave that is devouring most of our rights and safeguards in the name of empty promises of competitiveness and sovereignty.

On 21 October 2026, EU governments agreed on their negotiating position, which has timidly corrected some of the Commission’s most questionable choices, but has mainly endorsed changes that could make exploiting personal data easier while making abuses even harder to challenge.

title: EDRi-gram, 29 October 2026
content:
What has the EDRi network been up to over the past few weeks? Find out the latest digital rights news in our regular newsletter. In this edition: Celebrating end-to-end encryption, and the digital justice community in Europe and beyond

We’re still riding the high from October milestones showcasing the strength of our community. We had the pleasure of greeting many of you in person and online for #PrivacyCamp26 two weeks ago to discuss the origins of technology and how to pivot from conversations around “sovereignty” to meaningful, community-led self-determination. If you weren’t able to make it but you’re curious about the conversations, you can rewatch the livestream of some of the panel discussions.

Then, on October 21, we celebrated Global Encryption Day, highlighting end-to-end encryption as a crucial foundation to our right to safe and secure communication online and to life as we know it. Thanks to our members and partners, our message of protecting encryption was visible across several European capitals – from the metro trains of Prague to key landmarks in Berlin, Paris and Dublin with mobile “encryption trucks”. We also worked with European Sex Workers Alliance and Féministes contre le cyberharcèlement to raise awareness on the importance of safe and secure communications for sex workers as well as womens’ rights. author: EDRi
title: The internet should not demand constant self-defence: Fairness starts before the click
content:
A fair digital environment cannot – and should not – depend on everyone being permanently alert. Fairness must be built into the environment itself, not left to the skills of the people using it. In practice, that means rules, not appeals: cancelling must be as easy as subscribing, protection must be the default rather than a setting, and a system that detects a moment of weakness must not be allowed to act on it.

You open an app to answer one message. Twenty minutes later, you are still there. A video starts playing before you choose it. The next one follows automatically. A notification appears just as you are about to leave. Cancelling a subscription takes six steps. Signing up took one.

We often blame these experiences on bad habits, weak self-control or poor digital literacy. That lets the companies designing them off the hook. The truth is that many digital services are built to keep us watching, clicking, buying and sharing data. They test colours, wording, timing, rankings and notifications to see what hooks us most. They learn when we hesitate, when we are tired and what makes us stay. The resulting pressure is rarely accidental: it is the business model. In 2019, EU consumer authorities made Booking.com change practices including misleading scarcity claims, discounts and rankings. author: EDRi
title: What the new Convention on Decent Work in the Platform Economy means for workers – and what’s next for implementation
content:
In June 2026, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) adopted a new Convention on Decent Work in the Platform Economy. Following in the footsteps of the EU’s Platform Work Directive, this Convention extends data protection rights for platform workers and contains innovative provisions to protect against the adverse effects of automated decision-making globally. But this is only the beginning. In this article, EDRi member Privacy International explores what’s next for ratification, implementation and the future of regulating worker surveillance in the EU and around the world.

By Privacy International (guest author) · October 29, 2026

On 12 June 2026, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) adopted Convention C193 on Decent Work in the Platform Economy. This is a landmark piece of legislation as the first global legally binding instrument regulating the platform economy and addressing the impact of technology on the world of work.

The Convention represents a significant step forward for workers’ rights around the globe. It reflects the growing consensus that digital platform workers need more adequate protection from abusive and exploitative employment practices. It also reflects the need to regulate the use of automated decision-making (ADM) in the workplace affecting platform workers, an issue Privacy International has developed a set of recommendations on.

author: EDRi
title: Draconian access block orders in Turkey
content:
Court orders to block access to X accounts in Turkey reached an unprecedented number in September 2026. In this blog, EDRi-member Alternatif Bilisim detail the crackdown on civil rights defenders and independent media in the country, and call on public authorities to reconsider block orders and protect fundamental rights.

By Alternatif Bilisim (guest author) · October 29, 2026

Court orders to block access to X accounts in Turkey reached an unprecedented number in September 2026, followed by the closure of T24, an independent news website. According to data from the EngelliWeb project of the Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD), X blocked at least 1,270 accounts. In comparison, a total of 995 accounts were blocked in the entire year of 2025. In fact, the website of EngelliWeb, which tracks and documents online censorship in Turkey, was also blocked on 1 October 2026. Authoritarian measures and alarming levels of censorship in the country are increasingly eroding freedom of expression.

The common factor in all decisions related to access block orders is Article 8/A of Law No. 5651. This article allows the right of life, the safety of life and property of the persons, the protection of national security and public order, the prevention of crime or the protection of the internet contents or the prevention of access to the internet content. title: Surveillance in times of insecurity: a wicked and stupid strategy
content:
Sweden has been grappling with crime-related challenges in the past years. The difficulty to address violent crimes in cities notably has triggered extensive legislative reforms to increase surveillance and repression, including that of children. Tougher criminal penalties, widespread videosurveillance, mass electronic monitoring and government hacking are just a few examples illustrating the Swedish government’s attempt to counter public safety threats.

Sweden has been grappling with crime-related challenges in the past years. The difficulty to address violent crimes in cities notably has triggered extensive legislative reforms to increase surveillance and repression, including that of children. Tougher criminal penalties, widespread video surveillance, mass electronic monitoring and government hacking are just a few examples illustrating the Swedish government’s attempt to counter public safety threats.

However, this approach is not only misguided, as no evidence of its effectiveness exists, but also harmful to the fundamental right to personal integrity and thus to Swedish democracy. Furthermore, its impacts disproportionately fall on communities already marginalised and overpoliced.
